dimensions.name: Requirements clarification
dimensions.description: Separates browsing, holding, confirming, cancelling, and expiry, and states the assumptions that matter for correctness.

levels.1: Restates the prompt without identifying the hold or payment lifecycle.
levels.2: Lists the main actions but omits expiry, cancellation, or the no-oversell requirement.
levels.3: Separates functional and non-functional requirements and states clear assumptions about payments and event scope.
levels.4: Also prioritizes requirements, defines what is out of scope, and connects ambiguity such as seat transfer or waiting rooms to design consequences.

dimensions.name: Back-of-envelope estimation
dimensions.description: Turns the traffic and retention numbers into write QPS, read QPS, peak burst, and storage estimates.

levels.1: Repeats the given numbers without deriving anything.
levels.2: Computes average QPS but ignores peak bursts, seat-map reads, or storage.
levels.3: Estimates average and peak write/read rates and the storage needed for bookings and audit data.
levels.4: Also sizes cache working sets, per-event hot-spot load, and the capacity headroom needed for an on-sale.

dimensions.name: API and data model
dimensions.description: Defines hold, confirm, and cancel APIs with idempotency, and models seats and holds so double sale is impossible.

levels.1: Provides vague endpoints and no ownership model.
levels.2: Has endpoints for seats and bookings but omits idempotency or the hold entity.
levels.3: Defines request/response shapes, idempotency keys, and seat/hold/reservation tables with a uniqueness rule.
levels.4: Also explains the exact constraint or transaction that prevents double sale and how release, sold state, and audit records stay consistent.

dimensions.name: High-level architecture
dimensions.description: Places the reservation service, database, cache, payment worker, and expiry workers so responsibilities are clear.

levels.1: Shows a single service with no separation of reads, writes, or payments.
levels.2: Names components but does not show how a hold or confirmation flows through them.
levels.3: Shows the read path, the transactional write path, payment isolation, and expiry workers.
levels.4: Also explains why each boundary exists, how each component scales, and how events propagate to caches and workers.

dimensions.name: Deep dives
dimensions.description: Explains the atomic claim, hold expiry, and payment confirmation in enough detail to implement and test.

levels.1: No deep dive or only a restatement of the API.
levels.2: Covers one of claim, expiry, or payment and leaves the others vague.
levels.3: Covers all three with concrete transactions, locking, leases, or idempotency behavior.
levels.4: Also handles retries, races, and partial failures, and states the invariants each mechanism preserves.

dimensions.name: Trade-offs
dimensions.description: Compares the major choices and explains when an alternative would be preferable.

levels.2: Names one trade-off without connecting it to the design.
levels.3: Compares meaningful alternatives such as database constraints vs distributed locks, or synchronous vs asynchronous payment.
levels.4: Also explains the conditions under which the chosen option fails and how the team would revisit the decision.

dimensions.name: Communication and failure handling
dimensions.description: Presents the design clearly and covers failure modes, monitoring, and recovery.

levels.2: Understandable but omits several failure modes or recovery steps.
levels.3: Explains the flow clearly and covers payment, expiry, cache, and database failures with monitoring signals.
levels.4: Also presents degraded modes, invariant checks, alert thresholds, and a concise summary a reviewer can follow.
